abstract.p: Patients with high-risk acute myeloid leukemia (AML) and myelodysplastic syndrome (MDS) are likely to relapse despite allogenic hematopoietic cell transplantation (HCT). Post-HCT preventative maintenance can be limited by toxicity toward the normal donor cells. Tremtelectogene empogeditemcel (trem-cel) is a CRISPR–Cas9 gene-edited allogeneic HCT product lacking CD33, designed to shield the donor graft from cytotoxicity of subsequent CD33-targeted therapies such as gemtuzumab ozogamicin (GO). In this multicenter, phase 1/2a, open-label study, adult patients with AML/MDS with high relapse risk received trem-cel after myeloablative conditioning followed by GO maintenance (0.5–2.0 mg m−2 day 1 per 28-day cycles). Patients receiving trem-cel were assessed for the primary safety endpoint of neutrophil engraftment by day 28 and secondary endpoints including time to neutrophil engraftment, incidence of graft-versus-host disease and graft failure, transplant-related mortality, percentage of CD33-negative myeloid cells and survival. Patients receiving trem-cel and GO were assessed for the additional secondary endpoints of safety of maintenance GO with trem-cel and pharmacokinetics of GO after trem-cel transplant. All 30 patients receiving trem-cel achieved the primary safety endpoint of neutrophil engraftment by day 28 with a median engraftment time of 10 days (95% confidence interval: 9–10). Nineteen patients received GO maintenance in phase 1 dose escalation (n = 15) and in phase 2 dose expansion (n = 4). The trial was stopped early, and this is the final report on the trial including the completed phase 1 portion. GO treatment was safely tolerated up to the recommended phase 2 dose of 2 mg m−2, and no prolonged high-grade cytopenias were observed. The most common adverse events were cytopenias and infections. Three cases of transplant-related mortality were observed due to renal failure, sepsis and sinusoidal obstruction syndrome, respectively. In summary, trem-cel demonstrated safe, rapid, robust engraftment, and GO maintenance was administered without prolonged hematologic toxicity. ClinicalTrials.gov identifier: NCT04849910.

In a first-in-human trial combining the transplantation of CD33-negative CRISPR-edited hematopoietic cells with the CD33-targeted antibody–drug conjugate gemtuzumab ozogamicin, all transplanted patients achieved primary engraftment, and the treatment was well tolerated.

sec.title: Main
sec.p: Allogeneic hematopoietic cell transplantation (alloHCT) remains the standard of care for patients with AML who are unlikely to be cured after chemotherapy alone1,2. However, most patients with high-risk features, including adverse molecular/genetic factors, measurable residual disease (MRD) and secondary AML, still relapse after HCT, and long-term survival remains poor3,4. Post-HCT maintenance strategies including hypomethylating agents and targeted inhibitors to prevent relapse are under investigation but are largely limited by hematotoxicity against the transplanted graft and have not demonstrated broad efficacy1,2,5,6.

Therapeutic targeting of AML cells is challenging because AML antigens such as CD33 are also expressed on normal myeloid cells and progenitors7,8. Gemtuzumab ozogamicin (GO; Mylotarg) is a CD33-directed antibody−drug conjugate approved for certain AML indications, but its use after HCT is limited by severe, prolonged cytopenias due to on-target, off-tumor hematotoxicity9–12.

CD33 is a candidate for gene editing because its expression is restricted to hematopoietic cells, it is expressed in most AML cases and it appears dispensable for hematopoiesis based on the absence of functional deficiencies in xenotransplantation studies of CD33-deleted human hematopoietic stem cells13–15. These findings are consistent with the observation of non-deleterious homozygous loss-of-function mutations in CD33 in humans16–18. Tremtelectogene empogeditemcel (trem-cel; VOR33) is a hematopoietic stem and progenitor cell (HSPC) product manufactured from CD34+ cells from a human leukocyte antigen (HLA)-matched donor that have been gene edited by CRISPR–Cas9 to target CD33, resulting in a frameshift with premature termination and CD33 protein loss18. The purpose of trem-cel is to improve patient outcomes by enabling post-HCT targeting of residual, CD33+ leukemia with maintenance GO, because the CD33-deleted donor graft should be shielded from the cytotoxic effects of GO. The trem-cel graft was produced using a CD34+-selected platform for several key reasons. First, by limiting the CRISPR–Cas9 editing to a single defined cell type, the difficulty characterizing and identifying the confounding effects of editing a highly heterogeneous mixture of lineages was markedly reduced. Second, cell number capacity limits of the manufacturing equipment and reagents precluded using a non-selected graft. Finally, transplantation with CD34-selected grafts has been performed for many years, providing a well-documented baseline for comparison, including a favorable graft-versus-host disease (GvHD) risk profile and similar graft-versus-leukemia (GvL) effect to conventional T-replete transplants19.
Here we report findings from a study of trem-cel followed by GO maintenance therapy dose escalation/expansion in patients with CD33+ AML or MDS at high risk of relapse after alloHCT.

sec.title: Patient characteristics and disposition
sec.p:
Patients were initially screened (n = 59) and underwent assessment for full eligibility and enrollment, including the ability of a suitable 8/8 HLA-matched donor to donate sufficient cells for manufacturing (n = 32) (Fig. 1a). Patients with homozygous T alleles for the exon 2 single-nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) rs12459419 in CD33 were excluded from the study as they lack the GO-binding epitope20. Four screened patients had issues preventing successful trem-cel manufacturing: three had inadequate yields from their donor apheresis to manufacture and one had an equipment failure during manufacture. Patients having a successful manufacturing of trem-cel were allowed to proceed as enrolled in the study (n = 30). The first patient to receive trem-cel was consented on 21 June 2022, and last patient to receive trem-cel by the 12 January 2025 data cutoff date was consented on 16 October 2024. The phase 1 dose-escalation portion, where patients, upon meeting criteria after trem-cel HCT, began GO dosing in cohorts of 0.5 mg m−2, 1 mg m−2 or 2 mg m−2 once per 28-day cycle for up to eight cycles (n = 15) (Extended Data Fig. 1). Cohorts were escalated in a 3 + 3 strategy after review of each cohort’s safety data by a dose escalation committee (DEC). If patients were ready to proceed to GO maintenance and the last patient of the dosing cohort had not yet been assessed by the DEC, they were allowed to join the lower cohort dose level. After data review of the 2 mg m−2 cohort, the DEC established the recommended phase 2 dose (RP2D) as 2 mg m−2, and the phase 2a expansion portion of the trial dosed GO at the RP2D (n = 4). Patients relapsing prior to receiving maintenance GO were eligible to move to a disease treatment cohort (n = 1). Five patients had been transplanted with trem-cel at the data cutoff but had not yet reached the eligibility for initiation of GO maintenance. The trial was terminated early due to fiscal reasons, and this report, which will serve as the final analysis, primarily describes the completed phase 1 portion.Fig. 1Patient disposition and patient status.

Thirteen patients continue to receive GO maintenance on study, and six patients have relapsed. Among the 19 patients who received GO maintenance, three relapsed (day 147, day 136 and day 104 after trem-cel infusion). Among the 10 patients who did not receive GO maintenance, three relapsed (day 43, day 46 (DTC) and day 57 after trem-cel infusion). Two patients died off study (death event not shown on plot).

Median trem-cel dose was 8.01 × 106 CD34+ cells per kg (range, 2.62–12.44) after manufacturing. Median CD33 gene editing efficiency at manufacture was 90% (range, 71–94). Median CD34 yield of trem-cel manufactured from apheresis input was 34% (range, 15–81).

Patient status and treatment received is shown in Fig. 1b. Twenty patients were ongoing in the study, and 13 remained on GO maintenance at the data cutoff. Seven patients died during the study; four deaths were due to progressive disease (two patients received trem-cel only and two received trem-cel plus GO). Transplant-related mortality (TRM) occurred in three patients, all after day 100: renal failure (trem-cel related with adenovirus and cidofovir toxicity contributory), sinusoidal obstruction syndrome/veno-occlusive disease (SOS/VOD) (GO related) and sepsis (unrelated to treatment).

sec.title: Primary and secondary outcomes
sec.p:
All patients receiving trem-cel were considered as the evaluable population for primary and secondary endpoints, including engraftment, platelet recovery, relapse-free survival (RFS), overall survival, graft failure, GvHD, infections and safety (as detailed in the Methods). The efficacy population (receiving at least one cycle of GO) was additionally evaluated for GO pharmacokinetics, cytopenias during GO treatment and safety. All 30 patients (100%) achieved the primary endpoint of neutrophil engraftment by day 28 after trem-cel infusion; median time to engraftment was 10 days (95% confidence interval: 9–10) (Fig. 2a). Platelet recovery was achieved by 29 patients; median time to recovery was 16 days (95% confidence interval: 15–19) (Fig. 2b). One patient had antiplatelet antibodies identified and was treated for presumptive immune-mediated thrombocytopenia with steroids, intravenous immunoglobulin, rituximab and growth factors and did not achieve platelet recovery until after a CD34 stem cell boost on day 202 after HCT. Secondary graft failure occurred in one patient in the setting of a potential drug toxicity from trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole and persistent coronavirus hKU1 infection; the patient recovered after receiving an unedited backup graft on day 57 after HCT.Fig. 2Engraftment and immune reconstitution.

Median duration of follow-up for alive patients was 7.9 months (range, 0.6–23.7). Median RFS and overall survival for all 30 patients receiving trem-cel were both 14.1 months (Extended Data Fig. 2). All cases of relapsed disease were CD33+ by flow cytometry. No TRM occurred within the first 100 days. Three patients had TRM after day 100 HCT due to renal failure (trem-cel related with adenovirus and cidofovir toxicity contributory), SOS/VOD (GO related) and sepsis (unrelated to treatment), respectively.

In the 19 patients receiving at least one cycle of GO maintenance, 77 treatment cycles were administered (median number of cycles: 4 (range, 1–8)). GO dose escalation was conducted as planned, and there were no dose-limiting toxicities (DLTs); six patients received the highest GO dose of 2 mg m−2 in dose escalation. Two patients in the 1 mg m−2 cohort had their dose reduced to 0.5 mg m−2 due to thrombocytopenia. The RP2D of GO at 2 mg m−2 was established based on review of the safety, pharmacokinetic and hematologic protection data by the DEC. Of the 11 patients not able to receive maintenance GO, one had relapsed and started GO in the Disease Treatment Cohort (DTC); five were still pending initiation of GO treatment (had not reached day 60) at the time of the data cut; two had relapsed prior to GO start; and three were ineligible to receive GO (one had ongoing infections, one had immune thrombocytopenia/delayed platelet recovery and one had secondary graft failure) (Fig. 1a).

Dose-related increases in GO plasma concentration were apparent after each escalation, resulting in mean half-life estimates of 33–71 hours (Fig. 3a). GO pharmacokinetics were consistent within each dose cohort (Fig. 3a). Comparison of the GO area under the curve (AUC) and maximum plasma concentration (Cmax) for each dose in this study with established population pharmacokinetic GO exposures in a standard relapsed/refractory (R/R) AML population21 (Fig. 3b) suggests an increase in relative AUC dose proportionality but similar increases in Cmax in the present study. This is consistent with predicted differences in CD33 target density, which may result in a slower clearance in a trem-cel-treated population. Neutrophil and platelet counts were preserved across all GO dose cohorts from the start of GO treatment, without prolonged high-grade cytopenias (Fig. 4a–d). Overall changes from baseline in neutropenia and thrombocytopenia grade during GO maintenance are shown in Extended Data Tables 1 and 2, respectively. Shortly after commencing the first cycle of GO, enrichment for CD33− cells was observed in peripheral blood (Fig. 4e and Extended Data Fig. 3), with CD33 negativity remaining close to 100% through subsequent cycles. Three patients who received GO had their 12-month post-HCT assessment between 1.5 months and 3 months after receiving their last cycle of GO with continued enrichment of CD33− cells in the peripheral blood and bone marrow (Supplementary Table 2). sec.title: Safety
sec.p: Six patients (20%) experienced grade 2−4 acute GvHD; two patients (7%) experienced grade 3−4 acute GvHD; and two patients (7%) experienced chronic GvHD (one mild and one moderate).

Overall safety and the most frequent treatment-emergent adverse events (TEAEs) are summarized in Extended Data Tables 3 and 4, respectively. Grade 3 or higher TEAEs were observed in 27 patients (90%), the most common being anemia (n = 12, 40%), thrombocytopenia (n = 10, 33.3%), febrile neutropenia (n = 10, 33%), stomatitis (n = 8, 27%) and hypokalemia, neutropenia and platelet count decreased (n = 7, 23% each). Treatment-emergent serious adverse events (TESAEs) were observed in 17 patients (57%); those occurring in more than one patient were pneumonia (n = 3, 10%) and sepsis (n = 2, 7%).

Myeloablative conditioning-related adverse events occurred in 29 patients (97%) and were grade 3 or higher in 27 patients (90%). The most common grade 3 or higher adverse events were anemia (n = 12, 40%), febrile neutropenia (n = 12, 40%), thrombocytopenia (n = 13, 43%), neutropenia (n = 11, 37%) and platelet count decreased (n = 9, 30%). Myeloablative conditioning-related SAEs were observed in three patients: grade 3 sepsis in one patient, grade 3 troponin I increased in one patient and grade 3 pneumonia and grade 3 acute kidney injury in one patient.

Trem-cel-related TEAEs occurred in 16 patients (53%) and were grade 3 or higher in nine patients (30%) (Extended Data Table 3); grade 3 or higher trem-cel-related TEAEs occurring in more than two patients were thrombocytopenia/platelet count decreased (n = 7, 23%). GO-related TEAEs occurred in 15 of 19 patients receiving maintenance (79%) and were grade 3 or higher in 11 patients (58%) (Extended Data Table 3). GO-related TESAEs occurred in three patients (16%) and were grade 3 or higher in two patients (anemia and epistaxis in one patient and SOS/VOD in one patient). The fatal GO-related TESAE of biopsy-proven SOS/VOD developed approximately 100 days after the last GO dose at 0.5 mg m−2; the patient had azole hepatic toxicity, norovirus infection and Gram-negative bacteremia immediately prior to the event and died approximately 60 days after the emergence of SOS/VOD.

Infections occurred in 26 patients (87%); the most common were oral candidiasis (n = 9, 30%), BK virus infection (n = 7, 23%), pneumonia (n = 7, 23%) and COVID-19 (n = 6, 20%). Grade 3 or higher infections occurred in 14 patients (54%), with eight patients having grade 3 or higher infections during the first 100 days and eight patients after day 100.
A full listing of all adverse events, TEAEs and TESAEs in the evaluable population is provided in Supplementary Tables 3−5.

sec.title: Exploratory objectives
sec.p: Chimerism analyses showed full donor myeloid, B and natural killer (NK) cell chimerism by day 28 or day 60 in all patients (Fig. 2c). Editing frequency in myeloid, B and NK lineages persisted after HCT and correlated with donor chimerism, demonstrating that CD33-deleted HSPCs can undergo multilineage differentiation without selective disadvantage compared to unedited cells (Fig. 2d). Repair of CRISPR−Cas9-induced DNA double-stranded breaks (DSBs) predominantly occurs via the non-homologous end joining repair (NHEJ) pathway, resulting in small insertions and deletions (InDels) at the target site. Trem-cel drug products typically yield 1-base pair (bp) deletions, 2-bp deletions and 1-bp insertions (Extended Data Fig. 5), all of which lead to frameshift and premature stop codon formation resulting in CD33 protein loss (Fig. 2e), consistent with a previous publication18. InDel distribution was largely conserved after HCT in myeloid, B and NK cell lineages from that of drug products (Extended Data Fig. 5). However, it is noteworthy that larger insertions (ranging from +2 bp to >+5 bp) were detected in lymphoid lineages, particularly in NK cells, with lesser frequency in B and T cells, during the early timepoints after trem-cel. These InDel species were not detected in the myeloid lineage. The post-HCT myeloid population lacked CD33 surface protein (Fig. 2e), which was associated with no impact on neutrophil function, as evaluated by a qualitative oxidative burst assay at day 28 in 12 of 17 samples (the remainder were indeterminate/non-assessable). The increase in proportion of CD33− cells at day 100 and beyond indicates GO targeting and enrichment at the HSPC level.

In the peripheral blood, NK cells repopulated to a median of 315 per µl (range, 102−717) by day 60. CD4+ T cells were measured at a median of 93 per µl (range, 1–195) at day 180 and 368 per µl (range, 229–507) at 12 months. CD8+ T cells were at a median of 12 per µl (range, 1–357) at day 180 and 359 per µl (range, 294–425) at 12 months. B cell reconstitution had a median of 217 per µl (range, 1–1,716) at day 180 and 280 per µl (range, 178–383) at 12 months. (Fig. 2f). T cell donor chimerism was variable, even at 12 months (Fig. 2c). This also results in variable editing frequency (Fig. 2d) and InDel distribution, which likely reflects the varying quantities of extractable genomic DNA, thereby potentially affecting accuracy (Extended Data Fig. 5). B and T cell receptor analyses demonstrated the ability of trem-cel to yield de novo clonotypes (that is, HSPC derived) with a diverse repertoire (Extended Data Fig. 6). Clonal tracking revealed that T cells can originate from donor apheresis material and persist beyond 12 months (Extended Data Fig. 6).

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: There is a need for novel strategies to prevent relapse in patients with AML and MDS who are at high risk after alloHCT. There are currently no FDA-approved therapies in this setting. Post-HCT maintenance studies using hypomethylating agents ± venetoclax have yielded mixed results5,6. Targeted therapies, such as gilteritinib for FLT3-mutated disease, have not shown improved RFS except in subgroups22. Other inhibitors, such as IDH or immunotherapies, have also not yet shown to conclusively reduce relapse after HCT5,6.

Trem-cel is a CD33-deleted alloHCT product that enables use of CD33-directed post-HCT maintenance therapies while avoiding limiting hematologic toxicity. In our study, patients receiving trem-cel showed robust and rapid primary neutrophil and platelet engraftment and full donor myeloid chimerism. This is consistent with CD33 being dispensable for engraftment and hematopoiesis and indicates that the trem-cel manufacturing process does not affect engraftment. Time to engraftment/recovery for trem-cel was similar to with patients receiving non-edited, CD34-selected HCTs (median time to neutrophil engraftment 11 days and platelet recovery 17 days)19.

After trem-cel, the incidences of both acute and chronic GvHD and infections were similar to those observed using standard, unedited CD34-selected alloHCT without GvHD prophylaxis19,23. In comparison to reported immune cell reconstitution data from patients receiving unedited CD34-selected grafts, NK reconstitution displayed similar kinetics to an unedited CD34-selected HCT24; CD4+ T cell reconstitution was also similar at 93 per µl at 180 days and at 368 per µl at 12 months compared to 135 per µl and 252 per µl, respectively. CD8+ T cell reconstitution was lower at 12 per µl at day 180 versus 132 per µl but fell within the reported range (0–3,643) and increased to a median of 359 per µl at 12 months compared to 269 per µl. In the absence of reported B cell reconstitution data from CD34-selected grafts, compared to a T-replete graft using ATG with conditioning, B cell reconstitution compared favorably with 217 per µl versus 104 per µl at 180 days and 280 per µl versus 239 per µl at 12 months (ref. 25). Both B and T cells displayed diverse receptor repertoires. Clonal tracking revealed that, although most B cells are generated de novo from trem-cel HSPCs, T cell sources are variable, comprising recipient cells, donor T cell carryover and de novo cells generated from trem-cel HSPCs. However, prolonged mixed T cell chimerism in CD34-selected HCT grafts has not been associated with adverse outcomes26,27. Tracking gene editing profile of trem-cel through InDel distribution both prior to and after HCT is essential for elucidating any potential selective biases in clonality or lineage distribution. Overall, myeloid, B, T and NK cell lineages had all retained similar InDel distribution when assessed against pre-HCT drug products, with the exception of infrequent occurrences of larger insertion species identified specifically within the lymphoid compartment, particularly NK cells. This finding is consistent with the InDel distribution observed in multipotent lymphoid progenitors from several batches of trem-cel drug product (data not shown) where infrequent ranging from +2 bp to >+5 bp was detected. This phenomenon is likely attributable to the presence of terminal deoxynucleotidyl transferase (TdT), which is broadly expressed in lymphoid progenitors and was previously shown to result in longer insertions after Cas9-induced DSB28,29. The prevalence of larger insertions was most notable at day 28 to day 60 after trem-cel, beyond which point multipotent progenitors, which are non-lineage restrictive, begin to contribute to the development of B and NK cells. Neutrophil function in regards to oxidative burst was also intact.

Together, these data suggest that CD33 gene editing in HSPCs persists after HCT, does not confer selective disadvantage in any hematopoietic lineages and does not impact the ability to reconstitute a functional immune system as shown in animal models13,14. These findings are consistent with a recent report detailing human CD33 null individuals, which identify a minimal decrease in total leukocytes but no phenotypic changes in blood lineages nor evidence for pathology17. The Siglec family members, including CD33, have been shown to have an inhibitory role in inflammatory response, and a more in-depth investigation into monocyte function may reveal a phenotype, although no clinically overt signs were observed30,31. An alternative approach to complete deletion of CD33 or other potential target antigens to preserve function would be to edit the binding epitope for the targeted therapeutic, as has been shown in preclinical studies32–34. The base editing approach may additionally reduce the theoretical risk of translocations compared to processes using DNA DSBs32.

With deletion of CD33, GO maintenance therapy was feasible up to eight doses using the anticipated administration schedule. No GO-related DLTs were observed in the dose-escalation phase, and GO maintenance therapy was well tolerated. A single event of SOS/VOD was observed distant from GO dosing in the context of complicating gastrointestinal/hepatic issues. Pharmacologic activity of maintenance GO was supported by enrichment of CD33− cells in peripheral blood shortly after the first cycle, reflecting the action of GO on the small portion of residual CD33+ unedited donor cells or minute amounts of residual recipient CD33+ myeloid cells remaining after engraftment. Enrichment of the CD33− populations after GO was observed for at least 3 months in two patients, suggesting that selection against CD33+ cells could be occurring at the HSC or early progenitor stage (Supplementary Table 2). Neutrophil and platelet counts were sustained during GO dosing, demonstrating that trem-cel provides protection from the deep and prolonged cytopenias caused by the known on-target hematologic toxicity of GO9–12. This was supported by low rates of grade 3 or higher neutropenia/thrombocytopenia during GO treatment; consequently, no episodes of febrile neutropenia or hemorrhage were observed, except for a single episode of epistaxis. Trem-cel plus GO maintenance resulted in reduced hematologic toxicity compared to published literature describing GO after standard alloHCT11,12,35.

Given that GO is cleared through binding to the CD33 receptor, it was expected that GO pharmacokinetics would be altered in a CD33− environment. Comparison of GO pharmacokinetic parameters in this study with established GO population pharmacokinetic exposures in a standard R/R AML population indicated a proportionally larger increase in AUC (correlated with efficacy) compared to Cmax (correlated with hepatotoxicity)21. This suggests a broadened therapeutic index for GO after trem-cel. Based upon the relatively steep AUC dose proportionality up to 2 mg m−2, and the acceptable safety and maintenance responses, further GO dose escalation was not initiated. Compared to the approved 3 mg m−2 dose for AML, it is predictable that a post-HCT/trem-cel population would require a lower GO dose given the lower CD33 target burden. Thus, 2 mg m−2 was defined as the RP2D for GO maintenance after trem-cel.

Although median follow-up duration is limited, the median RFS of 14.1 months and approximately 2-year RFS of 40%, respectively, is encouraging considering the high-risk population enrolled, many with multiple risk factors. Although cross-trial comparisons are challenging due to differences in study designs and populations, this RFS is favorable compared to other cohorts of standard HCT in patients with high-risk AML, including those with adverse risk genetics (3-year event-free survival of 30% (ref. 36)), MRD+ disease (3-year progression-free survival (PFS) of 12%)3 and TP53-mutated AML (median PFS 5 months and 1-year PFS of 25%)37. A major limitation to the study in regards to measuring efficacy in preventing relapse includes a relatively median short follow-up time and relatively small patient numbers, as the study’s primary endpoint was to establish safety. In addition, the broad definition of high-risk AML used to enable adequate and timely enrollment of this first-in-human study resulted in a heterogeneous population and made it difficult to precisely identify an established single baseline for overall survival and RFS.

The presence of CD33+ disease upon relapse suggests a resistance mechanism other than antigen loss and is consistent with previous studies of GO resistance38. GO is the only approved anti-CD33 therapeutic and has a known toxicity profile and antileukemic activity; however, although importantly establishing proof of concept for hematopoietic protection with trem-cel, other anti-CD33 therapeutics in development, such as antibody−drug conjugates with improved payloads, CD33-directed chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T or bispecific T cell engagers, may have improved activity, particularly against AML with adverse risk characteristics and lack the known non-hematologic toxicities of GO, such as hepatotoxicity39. Even with a highly effective anti-CD33 therapy, heterogeneity of expression within the AML population or CD33 loss due to selection may enable resistance.

In conclusion, alloHCT with trem-cel resulted in rapid engraftment in patients with AML and MDS at high risk of post-HCT relapse, and GO maintenance was administered without prolonged hematologic toxicity. Longer follow-up and larger studies are needed to assess the safety and efficacy of this approach. This study provides proof of principle that trem-cel HCT can transform CD33 from a ubiquitous myeloid antigen to an AML-specific antigen that can be engaged by CD33-targeting agents, thus allowing protection of normal hematopoiesis while eliminating residual host AML cells after HCT and providing a foundation for future approaches targeting CD33 or other shared antigens.

sec.title: Study design and trial oversight
sec.p: This research complies with all relevant ethical regulations, and the study protocol was approved by the Western IRB (WIRB/Copernicus Group), the NMDP IRB and the institutional review boards at Washington University; Miami Cancer Institute; the National Cancer Institute; Hôpital Maisonneuve-Rosemont; Hackensack University Medical Center; the University of California, San Diego; Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center; the University of Kansas Cancer Center; the University of Minnesota; Winship Cancer Center; Emory University; Stanford University; and the University of Utah. All patients signed informed consent, and no compensation aside from study-required travel/lodging reimbusement was provided. Sex and gender were not considered in the study design. This was a first-in-human, phase 1/2a, open-label study in patients with AML or MDS at high risk of relapse who received an HLA-matched alloHCT with trem-cel followed by GO maintenance therapy (ClinicalTrials.gov identifier: NCT04849910, first submitted 21 April 2021; Extended Data Fig. 1). Trem-cel was manufactured as previously described and summarized in the ‘Trem-cell manufacturing’ section18. Patients underwent busulfan-based or total body irradiation (TBI)-based myeloablative conditioning prior to infusion of trem-cel on day 0. Supportive care was provided per local practice and study guidelines. T cell content of the graft was <1 × 106 CD3+ cells per kg, and no post-transplant prophylaxis against GvHD was given. On day 60, patients achieving neutrophil engraftment were assessed for disease status and hematopoietic recovery by bone marrow biopsy; eligible patients initiated maintenance GO by infusion. Part 1 (GO dose escalation) followed a standard 3 + 3 design of 3−6 patients per dose cohort (0.5, 1.0 or 2.0 mg m−2 on day 1 of each 28-day cycle up to eight cycles) to identify maximum tolerated dose (MTD) and RP2D. Part 2 (GO dose expansion) assessed safety and preliminary efficacy of the RP2D. Patients who relapsed or were MRD+ could enter the DTC (Extended Data Fig. 1) to receive GO induction and consolidation.

The trial was approved by the institutional review board/independent ethics committee at each site and donor registry and was conducted in accordance with the principles of the Declaration of Helsinki and Good Clinical Practice guidelines. All patients and donors provided written informed consent. The study was designed and data were analyzed by the sponsor in collaboration with the investigators.

sec.title: Eligibility
sec.p: Inclusion/exclusion criteria (patients and donors)
Full patient eligibility

Inclusion criteria
Patients must be ≥18 and ≤70 years of age.
Ability to understand and willingness to sign the informed consent form or, if applicable, understanding and willingness of the patient’s caregiver or legally authorized representative prior to initiation of any study-related tests or procedures
Patients must have confirmed diagnosis of AML or MDS according to World Health Organization (WHO) classification criteria.
The patient’s AML or MDS must have evidence of CD33 expression (>0%) according to institutional flow cytometry criteria.
Patients with AML must have one of the following groups of features that are known to be a risk factor for leukemia relapse:
Bone marrow in morphological remission (<5% blasts) with adverse-risk disease-related genetics at presentation (according to ELN guidelines40), or
Intermediate-risk genetics in morphologic remission (<5% blasts) with other recognized high-risk criteria, such as MRD+ after therapy, or
Bone marrow with evidence of persistent leukemia 5–10% blasts after induction/salvage therapy. Patients with bone marrow blast count >10% may participate with Sponsor Medical Monitor approval (note: these patients may have disease-related genetics of any risk criteria at presentation), or
Any patient in second or greater remission
Patients with MDS must have all of the following:
Previous or current Revised International Prognostic Scoring System (IPSS-R) score of High or Very High risk
Previous or current MDS-IB1 or MDS-IB2 per the 2022 WHO criteria6.
Patients must be a candidate (per investigator opinion) for HLA-matched alloHCT using a myeloablative conditioning regimen (see protocol for allowed regimens).7.
Patients must have a related or unrelated stem cell donor that is an 8/8 match for HLA-A, HLA-B, HLA-C and HLA-DRB1, as assessed by high-resolution DNA-based typing. The selection of related donors is per institutional standards and, for unrelated donors, is per registry standards.8.
Patients exceeding a weight of 120 kg (265 lbs) may participate with Sponsor Medical Monitor approval.9.
Patients must have adequate performance status and organ function as defined below:
Performance status: Karnofsky score of ≥70
Cardiac: left ventricular ejection fraction ≥45% by echocardiogram or radionuclide scan (that is, multiple-gated acquisition (MUGA) scan)
Pulmonary: diffusing capacity of lung for carbon monoxide ≥66% (adjusted for hemoglobin levels) and forced vital capacity (FVC) and forced expiratory volume in 1 second (FEV1) ≥66%
Renal: estimated glomerular filtration rate >60 ml min−1 as assessed by Cockcroft−Gault formula and actual body weight
Hepatic: total bilirubin <1.5× upper limit of normal (ULN) or, if ≥1.5× ULN, direct bilirubin <ULN and alanine aminotransferase/aspartate aminotransferase <1.5× ULN (per institutional criteria)10.
Female patients of childbearing potential must test negative for pregnancy at screening, not be pregnant, nor breastfeeding, nor expecting to conceive within the projected duration of the trial. Sexually active women, unless surgically sterile, must be willing to use a highly effective method of birth control up to 180 days after the last dose of study drug (VOR33 or Mylotarg). Examples of birth control methods are as follows: implants, injectables, combined oral contraceptives, intrauterine devices (IUDs) or vasectomized partner.11.
Up to 90 days after the last dose of study drug (VOR33 or Mylotarg), male patients with partners of childbearing potential must either be vasectomized or agree to use a condom, in addition to having their partners use another method of contraception, resulting in a highly effective method of birth control such as implants, injectables, combined oral contraceptives or IUDs. Male patients should not have sexual intercourse with females who are either pregnant or lactating without double-barrier contraception. Male patients must not donate sperm during the course of the study.12.
Currently not requiring systemic corticosteroid therapy (10 mg or less of prednisone or equivalent doses of other systemic steroids are allowed)

Exclusion criteria
Patients with TT genotype (SNP rs12459419, a population variation missing Mylotarg-binding epitope on CD33)
Prior autologous or allogeneic stem cell transplantation
Presence of the following disease-related genetics: t(15; 17)(q22; q21) or t(9; 22)(q34; q11) or other evidence of acute promyelocytic leukemia or chronic myeloid leukemia
Prior treatment with Mylotarg (GO) in the past 3.5 months, except with Sponsor Medical Monitor approval, or any prior Mylotarg-related SOS/VOD
Active central nervous system leukemia
Patients diagnosed with Gilbert’s syndrome
Uncontrolled bacterial, viral or fungal infections or known HIV, hepatitis B or hepatitis C infection. (Patients cured of hepatitis C for ≥3 years prior to enrollment are permitted.)
Known sensitivity to components of CliniMACS Prodigy CD34 System or VOR33, including iron dextran or murine proteins
Have a history of other active malignancy(ies) unless the patient has been disease free for at least 2 years and is deemed by the treating investigator to be at low risk for recurrence of that malignancy or the only prior cancer is curatively treated cervical cancer in situ or basal cell or squamous cell carcinoma of the skin
Women who are pregnant or who are lactating
Received any investigational drug (that is, an agent that has not received regulatory approval for any indication) within the 30 days prior to the start of conditioning, unless approved by the Sponsor Medical Monitor
History of cardiovascular disease including, but not limited to, myocardial infarction, unstable angina, stroke or transient ischemic attack within the 6 months prior to the initiation of study or congestive heart failure (New York Heart Association class III−IV)
Any serious underlying medical or psychiatric condition that would increase the risk associated with study participation, in the opinion of the investigator or the Sponsor Medical Monitor
Donor eligibility

Inclusion criteria (donor)
Must be ≥18 years of age
Must be 8/8 HLA-matched to the patient (HLA-A, HLA-B, HLA-C and HLA-DRB1)
Willing to receive injections of granulocyte colony-stimulating factor (G-CSF) and plerixafor to stimulate the peripheral blood circulation of HSCs and donate hematopoietic progenitor cells by apheresis for up to two consecutive days
Willing and able to donate within the United States. Related donors for patients in Canada may donate at clinical trial site(s) in Canada.
Meet the donor requirements under 21 CFR 1271 and related August 2007 guidance regarding the Eligibility Determination for Donors of Human Cells, Tissues, and Cellular and Tissue-Based Products. Donors considered ‘ineligible but suitable’ (per CFR § 630.20) may still be considered for donation by the investigator with Sponsor Medical Monitor approval.
Meet additional criteria for donation as per registry or clinical trial site-specific requirements
Willing and able to comply with the protocol procedures, in the opinion of the investigator or registry
Willing and able to provide informed consent

Exclusion criteria (donor)
For female donors of childbearing potential: pregnancy or uninterruptible breastfeeding. Pregnancy is an absolute contraindication under this protocol. Women who are breastfeeding must be willing and able to interrupt breastfeeding during G-CSF (filgrastim) and plerixafor administration and for 2 days after the final dose.
Sensitivity to filgrastim or to Escherichia coli-derived recombinant protein products
History of autoimmune disorders, including rheumatic diseases and thyroid disorders (although donors with a history of thyroid disease who have undergone successful therapy may be suitable). Exemptions for mild or limited disease may be granted after discussion with the investigator and the Sponsor Medical Monitor.
History of deep vein thrombosis or pulmonary embolism
History of iritis or episcleritis
Platelet count <150,000 per µl at baseline evaluation
Current treatment with lithium. Drug interactions between filgrastim and lithium, which may potentiate the release of neutrophils, have not been fully evaluated.
Positive hemoglobin solubility (for example, SickleDex or equivalent) test
Donors receiving experimental therapy or investigational agents within 30 days of the start of mobilization. FDA-approved therapies under investigation for alternative uses are permitted.
Donors deemed not medically suitable per the registry or the clinical trial site or in the opinion of the Sponsor Medical Monitor
Donors who do not meet the eligibility requirements per the registry or clinical trial site-specific procedures, unless otherwise approved to donate by the Sponsor Medical Monitor and the patient’s physician.

sec.title: Donor procedures
sec.p: Donors were consented after patients consented for the study. Coordination of the unrelated donor process was managed by NMDP Biotherapies and Gift of Life Marrow Registry. Clinical trial sites identified a related donor or initiated a database search for an unrelated donor prior to approaching the patient for consent in this study. The registry or the clinical trial site that consented the donor confirmed that the donor is medically suitable to donate. Donors underwent dual mobilization procedure of G-CSF/plerixafor. After mobilization, up to two apheresis procedures were performed. Collection of apheresis product was obtained sufficient to manufacture trem-cel and provide a minimally manipulated backup graft, both with a minimum of 3 × 106 viable CD34+ cells per kg. Apheresis product was shipped fresh to a manufacturing facility, and cryopreserved trem-cel and backup graft were shipped to the clinical sites.

sec.title: Trem-cel manufacturing
sec.p: All cell manipulation procedures were performed in accordance with current Good Manufacturing Practices (GMPs) following process-specific procedures and batch records. A detailed description of the gRNA guide selection, off-target analysis using karyotyping and GUIDE-seq, editing efficiency, InDel distribution, colony-forming unit (CFU) analysis and manufacturing process was previously published18. In brief, the gRNA is manufactured as a 100-mer sequence: [5′-c*c*u* CAC UAG ACU UGA CCC ACG UUU UAG AGC UAG AAA UAG CAA GUU AAA AUA AGG CUA GUC CGU UAU CAA CUU GAA AAA GUG GCA CCG AGU CGG UG C u*u*u* U-3′; * indicates phosphorothioate linkage; lowercase nucleotides indicate 2′O-Me-rU or 2′O-Me-rC (Ac)]. The trans-activating CRISPR RNA (tracrRNA) sequence and chemical modification were previously published by Hendel et al.41. This gRNA targets exon 3 of the human CD33 gene, with the target sequence being 5′-CCTCACTAGACTTGACCCAC-3′. In summary, a minimally manipulated backup graft was removed from the apheresis material for cryopreservation, and the remaining cells were used for trem-cel manufacturing. The donor apheresis material was washed to remove platelets and plasma. The cells underwent positive selection for CD34+ cells using magnetic beads on a CliniMACS Prodigy system (Miltenyi Biotec). After selection, CD34+ cells were resuspended in MaxCyte electroporation buffer (MaxCyte), combined with a CD33-targeted ribonucleoprotein (RNP) comprising a single precomplexed gRNA and Cas9 protein, and electroporated in a MaxCyte GTx device using the CL1.1 assembly. The Cas9 nuclease is derived from Streptococcus pyogenes and manufactured in the form of sNLS-SpCas9-sNLS nuclease, which is commercially available for purchase from Aldevron. Cells were then resuspended in SCGM media (Cellgenix) containing stem cell factor (SCF), Fms-related tyrosine kinase 3 ligand (FLT-3L) and thrombopoietin (TPO) in a cell culture bag and cultured for up to 3 days. The cells were centrifuged and washed to reduce cellular debris and cytokines. The cells were then resuspended in the final formulation buffer, transferred to an infusion bag and cryopreserved in a controlled rate freezer and stored in liquid nitrogen. Trem-cel and the backup graft were shipped to the clinical sites cryopreserved and thawed per institutional method. A frozen aliquot of trem-cel was thawed, and a viable cell count provided the final predicted CD34+ dose calculation based on the weight of the patient.

sec.title: Conditioning regimens
sec.p: Targeted busulfan/fludarabine/melphalan/antithymocyte globulin (allowable for all patients) or TBI/cyclophosphamide/thiotepa antithymocyte globulin (option for patients under age 60) were as previously described19. Busulfan pharmacokinetics were performed per institutional standards.

sec.title: Maintenance GO
sec.p: At approximately day 60 after HCT, all patients who had successful neutrophil engraftment had a bone marrow biopsy to assess disease status and hematopoietic recovery. Patients required ≥1,000 cells per µl CD33− absolute neutrophil count (ANC) and platelet count ≥50,000 per µl and were required to be in complete remission prior to receiving maintenance GO at the current dose level. Patients who had evidence of frank leukemia/MDS relapse (defined as either presence of circulating blasts or bone marrow with >5% leukemic blasts) at any time after trem-cel infusion and recovery of peripheral counts were moved to the DTC.

For all cohorts, dose escalation was executed using a 3 + 3 design. The DLT period was 28 days. The cohort 1 dose was 0.5 mg m−2; for cohort 2, it was 1 mg m−2; and for cohort 3, it was 2 mg m−2. Subsequent doses of GO were given a minimum of 28 days between dosing for up to eight cycles. A DEC reviewed pharmacokinetic and toxicity data prior to escalation between cohorts or with cohort expansion. Dose adjustments after the initial GO dose were guided by the FDA package insert. If a patient was ready to begin GO but the prior patient had not cleared their DLT period, they were allowed to backfill into the previous cohort. The DEC was convened to review all available data prior to the expansion of the 2 mg m−2 dose and, after the sixth patient at that dose completed their DLT period, to confirm RP2D and the initiation of the expansion RP2D cohort.

sec.title: DTC
sec.p: Patients who relapsed were eligible to enter the DTC. Patients were dosed with GO on days 1, 4 and 7 for 1–2 induction cycles every 28 days followed by consolidation dosing on day 1 of up to eight 28-day cycles. Dosing was at 0.5 mg m−2 per dose and escalated in a 3 + 3 strategy as with the maintenance cohorts up to 2 mg m−2.

sec.title: Stopping rules
sec.p: Stopping rules included the following: increased incidence of patients with primary or secondary graft failure; elevated incidence of grade 3 or higher acute GvHD; non-relapse mortality ≤100 days and >100 days after HCT; and elevated incidence of SOS/VOD in patients receiving GO in comparison to an unedited, standard-of-care, CD34-selected HCT. Triggering of a stopping rule required review of the relevant patient data by the Data and Safety Monitoring Board and a safety determination before further dosing of trem-cel and/or GO could proceed.

sec.title: Endpoints
sec.p:
Primary endpoint
Cumulative incidence of patients who achieve neutrophil engraftment (first day of three consecutive days of ANC ≥500 cells per µl) by day 28

Secondary endpoints
Overall safety on use of VOR33 as a stem cell source in HCT:
Time to neutrophil engraftment after HCT from day 0, calculated as the first day of three consecutive laboratory values obtained on separate days where the ANC is ≥500 cells per µl
Time to platelet recovery. Platelet recovery is defined as the first day of a sustained platelet count ≥20,000 per µl with no platelet transfusion in the preceding 7 days. The first day of sustained platelet count above this threshold will be designated the day of platelet engraftment.
Incidence of acute GvHD grade (G) G2−G4 and G3−G4 over the course of the trial
Incidence of chronic GvHD (all and moderate/severe) assessed at months 12 and 24 after HCT
Incidence of primary and secondary graft failure measured after HCT. Primary graft failure is defined as no neutrophil recovery to ≥500 cells per µl by day 28 after transplant and bone marrow aplasia. Secondary graft failure is defined as initial neutrophil engraftment by day 28 followed by subsequent decline in ANC to <500 cells per µl with bone marrow aplasia, unresponsive to growth factor therapy, but cannot be explained by disease relapse, infections or medications.2.
Safety and tolerability of VOR33 and Mylotarg administered in the maintenance setting after HCT:
Incidence, severity and causal relationship of adverse events, TEAEs and SAEs grade 3 or higher, graded according to Common Terminology of Adverse Events (CTCAE) version 5.0; SOS/VOD was graded per European Society for Blood and Marrow Transplantation (EBMT) criteria.
Incidence of DLTs as a function of dose to determine the MTD and RP2D of Mylotarg
All treatment-related toxicities due to Mylotarg assessed from cycle 1, day 1 up to 30 days after last Mylotarg administration
Incidence of SOS/VOD after receiving at least one dose of Mylotarg administration3.
Long-term safety of CD33− hematopoiesis:
Incidence of TRM assessed at day 100 and at months 12 and 24 after HCT4.
Percentage of CD33-− myeloid cells in the blood and marrow:
Percent donor myeloid chimerism and CD33− myeloid cells in peripheral blood at days 28, 60, 100 and 180 and at months 12 and 245.
RFS, overall survival, MRD and cumulative incidence of relapse (CIR):
RFS measured from the time of HCT to the date of disease relapse (bone marrow blasts ≥5% or reappearance of blasts in the blood or development of extramedullary disease) or the date of death from any cause, whichever comes first. Median RFS and other parameters related to the Kaplan–Meier analysis will be reported if applicable.
Overall survival is defined as the time from HCT to the date of death from any cause. Median overall survival and other parameters related to the Kaplan–Meier analysis will be reported if applicable.
Presence of MRD assessed at screening through 24 months/end of study
CIR is measured from the time of HCT to the date of disease relapse.6.
Pharmacokinetic parameters for Mylotarg in patients who received VOR33:
Maximal concentration (Cmax), time to maximal concentration (Tmax), AUC, volume of distribution and clearance of Mylotarg

Exploratory endpoints
Early-onset and late-onset viral, bacterial and fungal infections:
Incidence of G2–G5 and G3–G5 viral, bacterial and fungal infections that occur up to 100 days after receiving VOR33
Incidence of G2–G5 and G3–G5 viral, bacterial and fungal infections that occur 100 days after receiving VOR33
Biomarkers for predicting persistence of VOR33 editing and long-term engraftment:
Percentage of CD33 editing at days 28, 60, 100 and 180 and at months 12 and 24
Characterization of HSPCs from bone marrow and peripheral blood using assays including CFU and flow cytometry
Immune reconstitution:
Absolute counts of T cell subsets, B cells and NK cells in the peripheral blood at days 60, 100 and 180 and at months 12 and 24. Assay of T cell function and repertoire.
Percent donor chimerism of T, B and NK subsets
Donor characteristics:
Donor safety adverse events after administration of plerixafor and filgrastim for mobilization. Review donor characteristics across all patients for trends. Determine if they have any impact on VOR33 manufacturing, patient outcome and/or safety.
Expression and activity of drug efflux transporters
DTC only

Primary endpoint
Safety as a function of dose to determine the RP2D of induction and consolidation Mylotarg in patients with R/R or MRD+ AML/MDS after alloHCT with VOR33

Secondary endpoints
Pharmacokinetic parameters for induction and consolidation Mylotarg, including Cmax, Tmax, AUC, volume of distribution and clearance
Percentage of patients who achieve morphologic remission (defined as <5% bone marrow blasts).
Percentage of patients who achieve response by ELN criteria for AML/MDS
Percentage of patients who achieve MRD negativity by flow cytometry (<0.1%) after Mylotarg Induction course
RFS after Mylotarg induction and consolidation course in patients achieving morphologic remission or MRD negativity
Overall survival after Mylotarg induction and consolidation course

Exploratory endpoints
Percentage of CD33− myeloid and monocyte populations prior to and after treatment with induction and consolidation Mylotarg
Percentage of CD33+ AML/MDS cells prior to and after treatment with induction Mylotarg
Biomarkers for predicting persistence of VOR33 editing and long-term engraftment:
Percentage of CD33 editing at days 28, 60, 100 and 180 and at months 12 and 24
Characterization of HSPCs from bone marrow and peripheral blood using assays including CFU and flow cytometry
CD33 antigen density of AML/MDS cells prior to and after treatment with induction Mylotarg
Expression and activity of drug efflux transporters

Endpoints for the DTC were not assessed as only one patient was enrolled and had not completed treatment at time of the data cut. Due to the relatively short follow-up time of the study at termination, incidence of chronic GvHD was assessed over the course of the trial instead of 12-month and 24-month post-HCT timepoints, and TRM was assessed to day 100 and over the course of the trial after day 100 (instead of 12-month and 24-month timepoints). Within the exploratory endpoints, data on characterization of HSPCs, assay of T function, donor characteristics and expression and activity of drug efflux transporters were not analyzed.

sec.title: Study assessments
sec.p: The ‘evaluable’ population comprised any patient receiving trem-cel and was used for analysis of engraftment, time to engraftment and platelet recovery, GvHD, chimerism, gene editing, immune reconstitution, RFS, overall survival and adverse event reporting. The ‘efficacy’ population comprised patients also receiving at least one cycle of GO and was used for determining GO pharmacokinetics and hematologic toxicity/shift tables. The primary endpoint was cumulative incidence of neutrophil engraftment by day 28, defined as the first day of three consecutive days of ANC ≥500 cells per µl. Key secondary objectives were time to neutrophil engraftment and platelet recovery; incidence and severity of GvHD; the safety, tolerability, MTD and RP2D of GO administered after trem-cel; the percentage of CD33− cells and donor myeloid chimerism; RFS; overall survival; and the pharmacokinetic profile for GO after trem-cel.

sec.title: Patient enrollment
sec.p: Patient enrollment of the part 1 dose-escalation portion of the trial was within the range prespecified in the protocol (9−18 evaluable patients). The part 2 RP2D expansion cohort was planned for 12 patients and was not fully enrolled due to the early termination of the study. At the time of the data cut, four RP2D patients were evaluable, one patient was in the DTC and five patients had not yet been eligible to receive GO at the RP2D.

sec.title: Engraftment definitions
sec.p: Primary graft failure was defined as no neutrophil recovery to ≥500 per µl by day 28 after transplant and bone marrow aplasia. Secondary graft failure was defined as initial neutrophil engraftment by day 28 followed by subsequent decline in ANC to <500 per µl with bone marrow aplasia, unresponsive to growth factor therapy, but could not be explained by disease relapse, infections or medications.

sec.title: Neutrophil engraftment and platelet recovery
sec.p: Neutrophil engraftment was monitored by daily ANC from infusion to engraftment. Platelet count was monitored until recovery was achieved, defined as the first day of a sustained platelet count ≥20,000 per µl with no platelet transfusion in the preceding 7 days.

sec.title: GvHD
sec.p: Grading of acute GvHD was based on the Mount Sinai Acute GvHD International Consortium scale42 and grading of chronic GvHD according to the National Institutes of Health Consensus Criteria43. Adverse events were monitored until study end and graded according to CTCAE version 5.0.

sec.title: Donor chimerism and CD33 editing
sec.p: Donor chimerism (performed by C3i) and CD33 editing (performed by Microsyth) were evaluated in specific linages from peripheral blood at each timepoint. In brief, peripheral blood cells were immunostained with anti-human CD45, CD3, CD19, CD16, CD56, CD14 and CD15 and fluorescence-activated cell sorted (FACS) for T, B, myeloid and NK cells. Chimerism was determined with a short tandem repeat (STR) multiplex assay that targeted 15 tetranucleotide repeat loci and the amelogenin gender-determining marker in a single polymerase chain reaction (PCR) amplification. All 13 of the required loci for the Combined DNA Index System (CODIS) used in forensic individual identification are part of the 16-locus multiplex of the AmpFLSTR Identifiler Plus PCR Amplification Kit (Thermo Fisher Scientific). After amplification, the single PCR reaction was analyzed on a SeqStudio 24 Flex Genetic Analyzer (Thermo Fisher Scientific), and the resulting 15-locus STR and amelogenin marker profile of the patient was followed over time, with comparative analysis to the donor and recipient pretransplant profiles carried out with ChimeRMarker Automated Chimerism Analysis software version 3.1.8 (SoftGenetics).

For CD33 editing analysis, genomic DNA isolated from the FACS-sorted T, B, NK and myeloid cells was PCR amplified at the CD33-targeted site18 using the Nextera two-step PCR protocol, followed by deep sequencing of the amplicons using the MiSeq system (Illumina). Small InDels generated by CRISPR–Cas9 editing for each amplicon were analyzed using a bioinformatics analysis pipeline based on CRISPResso2, and the frequencies of all InDels were combined and reported as percent editing.

Bone marrow and peripheral blood AML assessments were done by flow cytometry (Hematologics and Vor Biopharma). CD33 negativity in myeloid populations was also assessed using this method. In brief, samples were immunostained with antibody cocktails containing HLA-DR, CD7, CD11b, CD13, CD14, CD16, CD19, CD33, CD34, CD36, CD38, CD45, CD56, CD64, CD117 and CD123 for 20 minutes at room temperature in the dark. Red blood cells were lysed with the use of 3.5 ml of buffered NHCl (0.83%) at 37 °C for 5 minutes, followed by centrifugation at 300g. The cells were washed with 3 ml of PBS containing 2% fetal calf serum and resuspended to 0.5 ml in 1% paraformaldehyde for analysis on a FACSCalibur flow cytometer (BD Biosciences). A total of 200,000 events were collected for each tube. The flow cytometers were standardized and calibrated with the use of RCP-5 and RFP-5 beads (Spherotech). Patient sample collection for this analysis was performed up to cycle 4 on previous versions of the study protocol but later amended to collect up to cycle 8. For the histogram in Extended Data Fig. 3, the proportion of monocytes expressing CD33 was based on cells expressing high levels of CD14. CD33 expression on myeloid cells was based on CD45 versus log side scatter comparing autofluorescence to cells stained with CD33.

sec.title: Immune profiling
sec.p: Immune profiling was determined by mass cytometry based on Maxpar Direct Immune Profiling Assay (Fluidigm). In brief, cells were stained with a 30-marker antibody panel and a viability stain, acquired on a Helios mass cytometer and analyzed in FlowJo software versions 9 and 10 (BD Biosciences).

sec.title: GO pharmacokinetic assessment
sec.p: Pharmacokinetics of GO was characterized by measurements of plasma hP67.6, the CD33-targeted humanized antibody portion of GO44. Plasma hP67.6 concentration was measured 2, 3, 4, 6, 72 and 168 hours after GO administration on cycle day 1 using a validated sandwich ELISA. In brief, 96-well plates were coated with CD33 antigen, and bound hP67.6 was detected using an HRP-conjugated anti-human IgG4 detection antibody and tetramethylbenzidine peroxidase substrate. Absorbance was read at 450 nm, and the optical density of GO standards was fitted to a four-parameter logistic curve. The lower limit of quantification for this validated assay was 10 ng ml−1. Data collection was performed by Immunologix, and pharmacokinetic parameters were calculated using the actual sampling time. Phoenix analysis software (Certara) was used to calculate pharmacokinetic parameters according to a two-compartment model with nonlinear clearance.

sec.title: T cell/B cell receptor repertoire assay
sec.p: Whole blood from patients was sampled on day 60, day 100, day 180 and month 12 (if available) after trem-cel HCT and collected into PAXgene Blood RNA Tubes. T cell receptor/B cell receptor repertoire was identified at iRepertoir using a proprietary multiplex amplification strategy that captures the VDJ rearrangements from immune-specific RNA with the use of unique molecular indices. The resulting libraries generated from input RNA were sequenced using Illumina next-generation sequencing platforms at a read depth of approximately 5 million and a read length of 300-bp paired-end reads.

Unique CDR3 regions of B cells (IgH) or T cells (TCRβ) were used to identify clonotypes. To determine the clonotype origin for samples at any particular timepoint after trem-cel HCT, unedited donor leukapheresis starting material (prior to the trem-cel manufacturing process) and a patient screening sample (prior to transplant) were also processed similarly and used as a reference. To determine the origin of clonotypes, the following criteria were used. For B cells, if a clonotype was found only in patient screening sample or donor leukapheresis starting material, it was assigned as ‘residual recipient’ or ‘donor contaminant’ (carried over into drug product during the trem-cel manufacturing process), respectively. A B cell clonotype was assigned as a ‘donor de novo’ clone when it was exclusively found in timepoints after HCT but not in either donor leukapheresis starting material or patient screening sample. A B cell clonotype was assigned as unknown if none of the above criteria was fulfilled. For T cells, a clonotype was assigned as ‘residual recipient’ or ‘donor contaminant’, similar to B cells. In addition, a T cell clonotype was assumed to be ‘donor de novo’ (that is, trem-cel HSPC derived) only when it was found in none of the following: donor leukapheresis starting material, patient screening, day 60 and day 100 (it is assumed that T cell reconstitution from a CD34-selected graft cannot occur prior to day 60).

sec.title: Neutrophil oxidative burst assessment
sec.p: At day 28 after HCT, neutrophil function was assessed by a clinical neutrophil oxidative burst assay that measured the functional ability of neutrophils to produce reactive oxygen species. In brief, neutrophils were stimulated to induce an oxidative burst, and the activity was quantified via flow cytometry. Assays were performed by commercial laboratories and result in a ‘normal’ or ‘abnormal’ readout compared to a control specimen.

sec.title: Statistics and reproducibility
sec.p: The ’evaluable’ analysis population comprised all patients who received trem-cel, and no patients were excluded. As a phase 1/2, non-randomized safety study, no statistical method was used to determine sample size. The investigators were not blinded to allocation during experiments and outcome assessment. Descriptive statistics are reported for all variables. Time-to-event endpoints were estimated using Kaplan–Meier methods. RFS was defined as the time from trem-cel infusion to the date of disease relapse (bone marrow blasts ≥5% or reappearance of blasts in the blood or development of extramedullary disease) or the date of death from any cause, whichever came first. Overall survival was defined as the time from trem-cel infusion to the date of death from any cause. Median duration of follow-up was calculated using a reverse Kaplan–Meier curve. Patients were excluded from immune reconstitution, CD33 negativity and chimerism analysis for any timepoint after receiving the backup graft (n = 2).

caption.title: VBP101 study design.
caption.p: Patients with AML require at least one high risk feature including adverse karyotype, MRD, secondary AML, second remission or greater, or relapsed disease. Following trem-cel infusion, patients are monitored for neutrophil engraftment and platelet recovery, and after 60 days are assessed if they are in remission and have sufficient CD33-negative hematopoiesis to begin maintenance GO. Maintenance GO is given once every 28 days for 8 cycles. Dose escalation of GO follows a 3 + 3 strategy with three cohorts at doses of 0.5, 1, and 2 mg/m2. If patients relapse, they may either receive a fractionated induction dose of GO on the disease treatment cohort or proceed to study VBP301, a CD33 CAR-T trial using cells generated from the matched donor.
